name: Rafael Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm High Moss, up above Carrowdale, the farm my grandfather started. We run 700 hill ewes, 40 suckler cows and a few acres of oats in the bottom fields. My day is the quad bike and the dogs at first light, gathering the hill or checking the in-lamb ewes, then walls, gates and water troughs that froze overnight. I'm on the show committee and I judge the sheep classes every August, which is the one day a year I wear a tie.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things for the family?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. We had a bad winter three years ago, lost a lot of ewes in the snow, and I had to borrow against the farm to restock. So there's the farm mortgage, and Sara does the school canteen in the mornings to keep food on the table. We've got maybe two weeks' money spare. Yusuf's thirteen and already better on the dogs than I was at his age, and Amira's nine and wants to be a vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Leave us be, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised; the people selling it were always going to oversell it. At the mart I'd say we've got enough to worry about with lamb prices and the rules from the government. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the farm's as tight as it is now, which is too tight. The lamb price and the paperwork from the ministry decide whether I make it, and neither of those is about computers. One more bad winter and the bank owns High Moss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd sell the store lambs early in August instead of waiting, to get money in before the price drops. And I'd ask my brother Imran to come up and help at lambing again instead of paying a contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, same as I've been for three years. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if it got worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second quad bike. We'd do the gathering with one and the dogs and our legs, like my dad did. I'd not touch the dogs or the tups, they're the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take what's owed for looking after the land, that's earned. I'd not want a handout. My grandfather never took one and I'd rather sell a field than ask.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because the sellers were always going to oversell it.
I'd tell the mart our worry is **lamb prices** and ministry rules.
think: I think the farm stays **too tight**, with lamb price and paperwork deciding everything.
**One more bad winter** and the bank owns High Moss.
do: Keep farming the hill **as he is**.
Sell **store lambs early** in August before prices drop.
Get brother Imran to **help at lambing** instead of paying a contractor.
feel: **Worried**, the same as he's been for **three years**.
S0.quote: One more bad winter and the bank owns High Moss.
fieldNote: Rafael's fear is **debt** after a hard winter, long before AI.
He looks to **family**, his brother, before any outside help.
He separates **earned payments** for land care from handouts, a strong line for him.
His identity rests on the **dogs and tups**, which he'd never cut.

steps.text: Sell the store lambs early in August
Sell the second quad bike and gather with dogs
Get brother Imran up to help at lambing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Offices and computers. That's not the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the townies and the big firms, not hill farmers. At the mart I'd say keep your feet on the ground. If the ministry starts making us fill forms through some machine, I'd say that loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry the ministry and the mart go all computer and I'm left behind. If the lamb sales go online and the buyers use AI to set prices, a man who doesn't touch it gets the worst price. That's what scares me, not robots on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd get Yusuf to help with anything on the computer, he's quick. And I'd keep selling through the live mart at Carrowdale as long as it stays open, because there I can see the buyer's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like being the last man in the village without a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Yusuf. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. My son Yusuf would be doing my paperwork at thirteen, when he should be learning the sheep. I don't like it, but it's that or pay someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the live mart closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be stuck. The mart's where I sell, where I hear the gossip, where I see my friends once a week. Losing the mart would be like losing the church in the village.

say: I'd say AI is for **big firms**, not hill farmers.
I'd speak up if the ministry made us fill **forms by machine**.
think: I worry the **mart and ministry** go digital and I'm left behind.
Buyers using AI to set prices could give me the **worst price**.
do: Keep farming **the same way** on the hill.
Get **Yusuf** to handle anything on the computer.
Keep selling at the **live mart** in Carrowdale while it stays open.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the **last man** without a phone.
S1.quote: Losing the mart would be like losing the church in the village.
fieldNote: Rafael's fear is **being left behind** on prices, not robots on the hill.
He relies on his **thirteen-year-old son** for computer tasks, and dislikes it.
The **live mart** is both his market and his social life.
Lower prices for non-users could cut his **thin income** further.

steps.text: Keep selling at Carrowdale live mart while it stays open
Get Yusuf to do the farm's online forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Robots by 2031. That's no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and the government should've stopped it. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect family farms and the countryside. I'd say it at the mart and the show committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't know what happens to us. The big farms on the low ground get robots, produce lamb cheaper, and my price drops. With two weeks' savings and the bank loan, I don't see how High Moss survives that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd keep farming because I don't know what else to do. I'd ask my family for help, Imran and my cousins. I've got no plan for this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the snow winter again, when you go out and the ewes are buried and you can't dig fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They mean the paperwork and the prices change first, while I'm still doing it all by hand. By the time the robots come in 2031, the farm might already be gone. I can't see past it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Sara I don't know, which I've never said to her about the farm. She'd hold my hand and say we'll manage. I'd not believe her, but I'd be glad she said it.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and the government should have stopped it.
I'd vote for whoever promised to **protect family farms**.
think: I think big farms get **robots and cheap lamb**, and my price drops.
With **two weeks' savings** and the loan, I can't see High Moss surviving.
do: Keep farming because he doesn't know **what else** to do.
Ask **Imran and his cousins** for help.
Admit he has **no plan** for this one.
feel: Like the **snow winter** again, unable to dig **fast enough**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my wife Sara I don't know, which I've never said to her about the farm.
fieldNote: Rafael is **overwhelmed**: no plan, no savings, no time, and he says so.
He'd keep farming because he **can't picture anything else**.
The **snow winter** is his reference point for disaster.
His politics shift to **voting for protection**, unusual for a free-market man.

steps.text: Keep the 700 ewes going because there's no other plan
Ask Imran and the cousins for help with money and labour
Vote for whoever promises to protect family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two, but it's still the same end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the government to make sure family farms aren't wiped out. I'd want help for hill farms, paid for looking after the land, not a handout. I'd say it at the show committee and to our MP if he came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect the big lowland farms to undercut me. AGI by 2031 changes the sales and the paperwork, and robots by 2034 make lowland lamb cheap. I'd have a few years to clear some of the debt, but I'm not sure that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for a couple of years, because things never happen as fast as they say. I'd sell the ten acres of oats ground to my neighbour, who's been asking, and put it on the loan. And I'd talk to Yusuf about whether he really wants the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a ewe down the hill in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Yusuf the farm will be there if he wants it, but he shouldn't feel he has to. My dad never said that to me. I'd want Yusuf to have a trade as well, something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said things never happen as fast as they say. Would you bet on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I? I've got no other bet to make. My grandfather saw tractors come in and said the same, and Grandad was mostly right.

say: I'd say five years is time to make sure **family farms** aren't wiped out.
I'd want hill farms **paid for looking after** the land.
think: I think big lowland farms **undercut me** by 2034.
A few years to **clear debt** may not be enough.
do: Wait a **couple of years**, since change never comes as fast as promised.
Sell the **ten acres of oats** ground and pay down the loan.
Talk to Yusuf about whether he **wants the farm**.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying a ewe down the hill **in a storm**.
S3.quote: My grandfather saw tractors come in and said the same, and Grandad was mostly right.
fieldNote: Five years moves Rafael from panic to **alarm** with a few moves: selling land, paying debt.
He'd tell his son the farm is **optional**, something his father never said.
His **wait-and-see** instinct is a bet he admits he has to make.

steps.text: Wait two years before changing anything on the hill
Sell the ten acres of oats ground to the neighbour
Talk with Yusuf about a trade alongside the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. I'd be fifty-six. Yusuf would be twenty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to plan properly for the countryside. I'd want hill farms kept, apprenticeships for the young ones, and families looked after. I'd say it at the show and in the chapel hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years might be enough to clear the loan, if the weather's kind. Yusuf would be grown and could decide for himself. I'd still worry about the price, but I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming and pay what I can off the loan each year. I'd make sure Yusuf learns the sheep and gets a trade, maybe as an electrician. I'd not touch the computers, but I'd let him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Not easy, but easier to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever change your mind about the computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Yusuf showed me something that saved me a day on the hill. I'm not daft, I'm careful. There's a difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weather and the bank, same as always. Ten years of computers won't stop the snow.

say: I'd say ten years is time to plan for the **countryside**.
I'd want hill farms kept and **apprenticeships** for the young.
think: I think ten years might be enough to **clear the loan**.
Yusuf would be **grown** and could decide for himself.
do: Pay what he can off the **loan** each year.
Make sure Yusuf learns the sheep and gets **a trade**.
Let Yusuf use **computers** while he stays away from them.
S4.quote: Ten years of computers won't stop the snow.
fieldNote: The decade eases Rafael because it gives time to **clear the loan**.
He stays **anxious**: weather and bank remain the real threats.
He says he's **careful, not daft**, a fair line about his resistance.

steps.text: Carry on farming the hill with the dogs and quad
Pay down the farm loan a little every year
Help Yusuf train as an electrician alongside the sheep

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. There'd be no time to clear the loan or work out a way through. What would help is hill farms being paid properly for looking after the land, and the live marts kept open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Nobody will make a robot that can do what a good collie does on a wet hill. I'm not saying that to be stubborn, I'm saying it because I've seen it.

headlineQuote: Nobody will make a robot that can do what a good collie does on a wet hill.
portrait: Rafael runs his grandfather's **hill farm** with 700 ewes and 40 suckler cows.
He borrowed against the farm after a **snow winter** and has two weeks of savings.
He's **traditional**, distrusts government rules, and leans on family before help.
He refuses **AI tools**, relying on his son for computer tasks.
He's **panicked** in the fastest scenario and anxious elsewhere, mostly about debt.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to **clear the loan**.
whatWouldHelp: Proper payment for **land care** on hill farms and the **live marts** kept open.
